image.prompt: Inside a modest Ethiopian living room with plain painted walls, a window with thin curtains, and simple cushioned seats along the walls, on Fasika morning. The mother sits on a low wooden stool, knees together, leaning slightly forward. On the floor at her side: a small round terracotta charcoal brazier about knee high, open at the top and full of glowing orange charcoal, standing on a round metal tray on the floor. She holds a flat round shallow metal roasting pan with a long straight metal handle, held just above the coals, full of coffee beans turning from light brown to dark brown, stirred with a thin wooden stick. In front of her: a rekebot: a small low wooden coffee table about knee height, shaped like an open box, dark brown wood with simple carved geometric patterns on its sides, its flat top holding two or three neat rows of sini cups; next to it, a jebena: a traditional hand-made black clay coffee pot with a round belly about the size of a small melon, a long thin neck rising straight up from the top, a short spout coming out of the side near the bottom of the neck, and a curved handle joining the neck to the belly; it stands upright on a small round woven straw ring. Nearby, a small terracotta incense burner shaped like a tiny goblet on a short stem, glowing charcoal and frankincense inside, giving off a thin curl of white smoke. The floor around the coffee area is covered with ketema: freshly cut grass, long thin bright-green blades like chives, each about an arm's length, scattered loosely and lying flat on the indoor floor, crossing each other in a light layer, the floor visible between the blades; it is cut grass spread on a floor, not a lawn, no soil, nothing growing. Warm golden morning light from the window, smoke rising softly. Not in the picture: no mugs, no cups with handles, no saucers, no metal kettle, no teapot, no iron or wood-burning stove, no lawn, no Christmas tree, no Western decorations
